chunks: What I2C is and what it stands for. The question: What is I2C? What does it stand for?
I2C stands for Inter-Integrated Circuit. It is a bus (a shared set of wires), just two wires, that lets many chips on one board talk to a controller.
One wire carries a clock, SCL, and one carries data, SDA. Every chip has its own address, so the controller says whom it wants and only that chip answers.
It is slow, from 100 kilohertz up to about 1 megahertz, so it suits sensors, memories and clocks that need few bytes.
Picture a single street with numbered houses. A delivery truck uses two lanes: one for the beat, one for packages.
The truck calls out a house number, and only that resident answers "got it". Each lane has a gate that anyone can pull down but nobody can push up.
A spring lifts it again when everyone lets go, so no two houses can ever fight over it. The spring is the pull-up resistor.
Every device taps into the same two lines. There is one pull-up per line for the whole bus (not per device), and the addresses (for example 0x48, 0x50, 0x68) tell targets apart.
The controller is simply the device that starts the transaction.
SCL and SDA: the clock wire and the data wire of the bus. Open-drain: an output that can only pull the wire low. A resistor makes it high ("Advantages of open-drain outputs").
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts the wires to high when nobody pulls them low ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size").
Controller and target: the chip that starts a transfer, and the chip that answers. Older documents say master and slave. Address: a 7-bit number that picks one target.
ACK: a reply bit from the receiver meaning "got it."
A controller writes the value 0x3 amps to a chip at address 0x48 ("0x" marks a hexadecimal, base-16, number).
It sends a START signal, then the address 0x48 plus a "write" bit, and the chip replies with an ACK.
Then it sends the byte 0x3 amps, gets another ACK, and finishes with a STOP signal. The two bytes take 18 clock ticks, about 180 microseconds at 100 kilohertz.
That is the whole idea.
"I2C stands for Inter-Integrated Circuit.
It's a two-wire serial bus, SCL for the clock and SDA for data, both open-drain with pull-up resistors, invented by Philips for connecting chips on one board.
Each device has an address, the controller sends START, address and read/write bit, the target ACKs, then bytes follow, each ACKed, until STOP.
It's slow, 100 to 400 kilohertz typically, but lets many devices share two pins."
